package_info.package_manager: Trojan-downloader (Windows malware, not a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (malware family, not versioned as a package)
package_info.why_malicious: Stantinko is a sophisticated malware family distributed via software bundling, primarily targeting Windows systems. It operates as adware and a botnet, performing browser hijacking, click fraud, and large-scale brute-force attacks against Joomla and WordPress sites. Its activities are intentionally deceptive, unauthorized, and cause harm to both end users and web services by enabling further malware delivery, credential theft, and unauthorized system control.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, after the user installs bundled freeware and the malicious binary is executed automatically on system startup.
execution_context.file_location: C:\Program Files\Stantinko\stantinko.exe (or similarly named Windows executable installed via software bundling)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Injected browser extension or process that programmatically modifies browser settings, redirects browser traffic to attacker-controlled domains, manipulates search results, and injects advertisements into web pages by altering browser memory or configuration files.
malicious_snippets.code_language: C++/JavaScript (native Windows binary with browser manipulation components)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code executes as a persistent background process, programmatically modifies browser settings and injects scripts into browser processes, redirecting user traffic to attacker-controlled ad or malicious domains and injecting advertisements into web pages, resulting in click fraud and enabling further malware delivery.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs unauthorized browser manipulation, including redirecting user traffic and injecting ads, which are hallmark behaviors of adware and malware. These actions occur without user consent and are designed to generate fraudulent ad revenue and facilitate further compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not alter browser settings, redirect user traffic, or inject advertisements into web pages without explicit user permission and transparency. Such actions violate user trust and system integrity.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some browser extensions may inject scripts for ad-blocking or UI enhancement, but only with user consent, clear disclosure, and adherence to browser security policies.
key_indicators: Unauthorized modification of browser settings or configuration files
Injection of scripts or DLLs into browser processes
Redirection of browser traffic to attacker-controlled or ad fraud domains
Persistence via registry or startup folder entries

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, as a background process after the malware binary is installed and persists on the system.
execution_context.file_location: C:\Program Files\Stantinko\stantinko.exe (or similarly named installed malware binary)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Automated brute-force module that systematically targets Joomla and WordPress admin login pages by sending repeated HTTP POST requests with different credential combinations, attempting to gain unauthorized access to web admin accounts.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code operates as a background process, initiates automated brute-force attacks by sending high-frequency HTTP POST login attempts to remote Joomla and WordPress admin panels over the network, aiming to compromise web admin credentials and expand botnet control.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated brute-force attacks against remote web admin panels are a classic sign of botnet and malware activity, as they attempt to gain unauthorized access to web services without user knowledge or consent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal software should not initiate repeated login attempts to remote web admin panels without explicit user initiation or authorization. Such behavior is only acceptable in controlled, authorized security assessments.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Penetration testing tools may perform similar brute-force actions, but only in authorized security assessments with explicit permission from the system owner.
key_indicators: High-frequency, automated login attempts to Joomla/WordPress admin panels
Network traffic patterns consistent with brute-force attacks (e.g., repeated HTTP POSTs with varying credentials)
No user interaction required for attack initiation
Outbound connections to known Stantinko C&C infrastructure

attack_chain.action: User downloads and installs freeware that is bundled with the Stantinko malware, often without clear disclosure.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware binary is silently installed and establishes persistence on the system.

attack_chain.action: Stantinko executes as a persistent background process, hijacking the browser and injecting advertisements by modifying browser settings and injecting scripts.
attack_chain.leads_to: Click fraud, unauthorized ad revenue generation, and potential delivery of additional malware via malicious redirects.

attack_chain.action: Stantinko initiates automated brute-force attacks against Joomla and WordPress admin login pages from the infected host.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential compromise of web admin accounts, enabling further botnet expansion and control over additional web resources.

behavioral_signatures: Unauthorized modification of browser settings or injection of scripts/DLLs into browser processes
Unexpected installation of browser extensions or plugins without user consent
Automated, high-frequency login attempts to Joomla/WordPress admin panels from user endpoints
Persistence mechanisms such as registry run keys or startup folder entries for unknown executables
Network traffic to known Stantinko C&C infrastructure or ad fraud domains
file_indicators: Presence of stantinko.exe or similarly named binaries in Program Files or AppData directories
Unexpected browser extensions or DLLs injected into browser processes
Persistence mechanisms in Windows registry (e.g., HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run) or startup folders
Modified browser configuration files (e.g., Chrome/Firefox profiles) indicating unauthorized changes
network_indicators: Outbound connections to Stantinko C&C servers (as identified in threat intelligence feeds)
High volume of HTTP POST requests to Joomla/WordPress login pages from a single endpoint
Traffic to domains or IPs associated with ad fraud or click-fraud operations
Encrypted or obfuscated network traffic patterns consistent with C&C communication
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for unauthorized changes to browser settings, unexpected browser extensions, or injected scripts/DLLs. Detect high-frequency login attempts to remote Joomla/WordPress admin panels originating from user endpoints. Scan for the presence of stantinko.exe or similarly named binaries and persistence mechanisms in the registry or startup folders. Analyze outbound network traffic for connections to known Stantinko C&C infrastructure, ad fraud domains, and patterns indicative of brute-force attacks. Correlate behavioral, file, and network indicators to identify and respond to Stantinko infections.
